design_detail: Systematic review (19 studies, 1970 to 2016) with inverse-variance meta-analyses in RevMan 5.3 (Hedges' g) of next-day cognitive performance after an evening of heavy drinking. Only studies with a no-hangover control condition, a measure validating the hangover (a symptom questionnaire) and blood alcohol near zero at testing (threshold in the exposure field) were eligible. Five pooled analyses (sustained attention, divided attention, short-term memory, long-term memory, psychomotor speed), each of four or five studies; 11 studies contributed to at least one. PROSPERO CRD42017054617.
can_establish: Whether healthy adults tested the morning after heavy drinking, with blood alcohol near zero, performed worse on attention, memory and reaction-time tasks than on a control day in the small controlled literature to 2016, and roughly how large the average difference was in standardized units.
cannot_establish: What the difference means for everyday tasks (effects are standardized and no task is tied to a real-world outcome except three simulator driving studies that were not pooled); whether the impairment comes from alcohol itself rather than lost sleep, expectation or fatigue (sleep, food and smoking were not controlled in the naturalistic studies); whether people who drink heavily but feel no hangover are affected (no separate analysis); how impairment changes with the amount drunk (no dose-response analysis); and whether the pooled estimates are inflated by small-study or publication effects (not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Searches of PubMed, Embase and PsycNET run between December 2016 and May 2018 with terms for alcohol and hangover, plus reference lists of articles; no date limit (included studies date from 1970 to 2016). The review does not tabulate where participants came from; the reference titles of included studies name college students (Howland et al., 2010), maritime academy cadets (Rohsenow et al., 2006) and young adults (Rohsenow et al., 2010), and one study was of women only (Kruisselbrink et al., 2006).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: healthy adults aged 18 or over; a no-hangover control condition; a measure validating the presence of hangover; blood alcohol concentration (BAC) near zero at testing (threshold in the exposure field); laboratory (alcohol given) or naturalistic (drinking at a time and place of the person's choosing) designs. Of 20 articles excluded at full text, the stated reasons were: no hangover measure at testing (12 studies), only fatigue or arousal found on the hangover measure (2), no BAC at testing (7), BAC above the threshold (2), another treatment in the design (2), and data already included (1). These reasons sum to 26 for 20 articles, so several studies were excluded for more than one reason.
sample.demographics: Not tabulated beyond per-study n (5 to 193), design, alcohol dose and BAC at testing (Table 1). Several studies averaged the dose across men and women; age, sex mix and country are not given for most studies.
sample.attrition: 1163 participants recruited across the 19 studies (assuming no attrition where none was reported) and 846 with data reported, an attrition of 27.3% (Results › Identification of studies, 2nd paragraph). The Table 1 sample sizes sum to 846 at their upper bounds (editors' arithmetic).
sample.selection_effects: The strict definition (validated hangover, near-zero BAC) removed several studies with null results that the Introduction cites: Finnigan et al. (1998), Chait and Perry (1994) and Lemon et al. (1993) were excluded at full text, two of them because the hangover measure showed only fatigue or arousal, that is, on the strength of the hangover the study produced. Four other null studies cited in the Introduction (Carroll et al., 1964; Ideström and Cadenius, 1968; Morrow et al., 1990; Dowd et al., 1973) do not appear among the full-text exclusions, so how they were handled is not reported. In naturalistic studies people were tested after nights on which they chose to drink heavily, so the sample is people who drink heavily and agreed to be tested the next morning. Two included studies had some participants above the blood alcohol limit (Törnros and Laurell, 1991, at their earliest morning session; four participants in Verster et al., 2014).

exposure.measurement: An evening of heavy drinking before testing: alcohol given in the laboratory, or drinking chosen by the participants in naturalistic studies, with intake self-reported or peak BAC estimated. The hangover was validated by a questionnaire (Acute Hangover Scale, a 20-item hangover questionnaire, rated severity and others) and BAC was measured at testing.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated (Table 1): laboratory studies 0.8 to 1.43 g/kg, naturalistic studies 1.25 to 1.77 g/kg; the Discussion gives means of 1.21 g/kg (laboratory) and 1.54 g/kg (naturalistic). One Table 1 entry reads 13 g/kg (Collins and Chiles), evidently a typesetting error. A single drinking episode, by mouth.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed beyond the limitation that three studies did not control nicotine use (Myrsten et al., 1970; Collins, 1980; Collins and Chiles, 1980). Other drug use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: BAC below 0.02% at testing by inclusion (0 to 0.012% in Table 1), with two exceptions: some participants above 0.02% at the 9 a.m. session in Törnros and Laurell (1991), and four participants in Verster et al. (2014). The time between drinking and testing, and the sleep allowed, varied between studies and are not tabulated; the authors state this makes firm conclusions difficult.

comparison.controls: A no-alcohol, placebo or no-drinking control day for the same people in most studies (within-person designs); a separate no-hangover group in the mixed designs (Finnigan et al., 2005; McKinney and Coyle, 2007; Rohsenow et al., 2006; Rohsenow et al., 2010).
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison in most studies. Condition order was not randomized in one study (Kim et al., 2003) and task order was not randomized in three (McKinney and colleagues).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Largely not relevant for within-person comparisons. Not controlled in naturalistic studies, and not assessed by the review: sleep duration and timing, food, expectation and the motivation to perform after a night out.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Nicotine use not controlled in three studies; other drugs not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Tasks were coded into cognitive components: sustained attention (Psychomotor Vigilance Task, Continuous Performance Test, a correction test, sustained-attention tasks), divided attention (tracking with reaction time, dual task), selective attention (flanker, Stroop), vigilance (Mackworth clock), working memory (adaptive paced auditory serial addition, visual span and auditory digit span backwards), short-term memory (word recall, probed recall, pattern memory, pattern identification), long-term memory (delayed recall and recognition, lecture material learned while sober), psychomotor speed (simple and choice reaction time), psychomotor accuracy, and real-life simulations (simulated driving, ship power-plant operation, managerial simulation, graduate record examination).
outcomes.validity_norms: Two studies used tasks from the Neurobehavioral Evaluation System 3, validated for detecting cognitive impairment; the authors note that several other tasks had never been shown to be sensitive to drug-induced state changes.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment means poorer performance (slower, less accurate, fewer items recalled) after heavy drinking than in the control condition, expressed as Hedges' g with positive values meaning worse performance in the hangover condition. Several outcomes from one study within the same component were averaged so that no study counted twice.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across the five pooled analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Screening by two independent reviewers (95% agreement); data extraction is not described as done in duplicate. Blinding of participants was not counted as a risk of bias because, the authors say, participants readily guess their condition.

analysis.effect_sizes: Hedges' g with 95% CI, studies weighted by inverse variance (RevMan 5.3); fixed- or random-effects model not stated. Short-term memory g = 0.64 (0.15 to 1.13), 5 studies, I2 = 73%, P = 0.01; long-term memory g = 0.59 (0.01 to 1.17), 4 studies, I2 = 84%, P = 0.05; sustained attention g = 0.47 (0.07 to 0.87), 4 studies, I2 = 50%, P = 0.02; psychomotor speed g = 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00), 5 studies, I2 = 36%, P < 0.001; divided attention, 4 studies, described as showing no evidence of an effect with no estimate given. No tau-squared, prediction intervals, subgroup analyses or tests for small-study effects.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; laboratory and naturalistic studies were pooled together.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42017054617, printed under the heading 'Pre-registered hypothesis'. The paper does not compare its methods with the registered protocol or report deviations; the record itself was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The divided-attention pooled result has no number. The four studies pooled for sustained attention are not identified in the text (two reference numbers are cited; Figure 3 is an image). One laboratory study with a null reaction-time result (Kruisselbrink et al., 2006) could not be pooled for lack of data, which the authors say may inflate the psychomotor-speed estimate.
analysis.power: Not addressed for the meta-analyses. Several laboratory studies had 5 to 15 participants; the authors name low power as a likely reason for null results and recommend a priori power analysis.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Each pooled estimate rests on four or five small studies. The morning after heavy drinking, with blood alcohol near zero, performance was worse than on control days by about half to two-thirds of a standard deviation for short-term memory, long-term memory, sustained attention and reaction-time speed, with wide intervals (the long-term memory interval reaches down to 0.01) and moderate to high heterogeneity (I2 36% to 84%). Divided attention showed no detectable effect, working memory was mixed, and the executive tasks (ship power-plant operation, a managerial simulation, examination scores) showed no clear effect. Two of three naturalistic simulator studies found poorer vehicle control, and one found no change in speed. Naturalistic studies, with more alcohol, tended to find impairments where laboratory studies often did not.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that hangovers "may involve impaired cognitive functions and performance of everyday tasks such as driving", which is suitably hedged. Gaps: (1) the abstract says 1163 participants across 19 studies were included in the analysis, while 846 had data and 11 studies entered any pooled analysis; (2) the abstract says the review suggested impaired driving, which was not meta-analysed and rests on three naturalistic studies, one of them null; (3) the Discussion explains null results by insensitive tasks and low power but does not weigh the same design weaknesses (sleep not controlled, unblinded naturalistic designs, non-randomized task order) against the positive results; (4) the Introduction states that the review examines next-day effects of heavy drinking rather than hangover as such, because people in the hangover conditions may have had no symptoms, a qualification absent from the title and abstract.

timeline.event: Stephens et al. and Prat et al. narrative reviews of the cognitive effects of hangover (cited as earlier reviews that excluded studies with any alcohol at testing).
Alcohol Hangover Research Group consensus statement on best practice (Verster et al., 2010), the basis of this review's inclusion criteria.
This review: by the authors' account the first to pool effect sizes for next-day cognitive effects.
Alford et al. simulated commute driving at zero and residual blood alcohol, a later primary study on the driving question the review could not pool.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of this question that its authors knew of. Its estimates are averages of a handful of small studies, mostly from three groups (Howland and Rohsenow; McKinney and Coyle; Verster), and the Howland et al. (2010) and Rohsenow et al. (2010) studies used the same test battery in the same group, without the review saying whether their samples overlap. The driving evidence it summarises is three naturalistic simulator studies (Laurell and Törnros, 1983; Törnros and Laurell, 1991; Verster et al., 2014), not pooled.

funding.funder: University of Bath research studentship. The acknowledgements also list funding from the British Heart Foundation, Cancer Research UK, the Economic and Social Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the National Institute for Health Research under the UK Clinical Research Collaboration.
funding.declared_conflicts: S.A. and M.R.M. are members of the UK Centre for Tobacco and Alcohol Studies; the other authors declare no relevant conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors thank R. Stephens and J. Grange, authors of an included study (Grange et al., 2016), for providing information, and obtained unpublished information from the authors of Verster et al. (2014) by correspondence.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered randomized crossover study in which the same people drink a measured amount of alcohol or a placebo in the evening, with sleep duration and timing held equal and measured, food and smoking controlled, and validated state-sensitive tasks plus a standard driving test given at zero blood alcohol the next morning, with hangover severity recorded and analysed as a moderator; and an updated meta-analysis with random-effects pooling, separate laboratory and naturalistic estimates, and small-study tests.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Healthy adults; heavy drinking the evening before with validated hangover and BAC near zero at testing; a no-hangover control condition; cognitive performance.
PROSPERO CRD42017054617 is cited, but the paper neither reports deviations nor compares its methods with the record; the record was not read, so whether it specified the analysis plan is not known.
The Introduction explains why laboratory and naturalistic designs were both included and why studies needed a hangover measure and near-zero BAC.

Three databases with the search terms given, reference lists searched, no stated language or date restriction, and the search ended three months before publication; but no trial registries, no stated grey-literature search and no stated consultation of experts (though authors were contacted for data).
Two independent reviewers screened, with 95% agreement and disagreements resolved by discussion.
Not described: the Methods say only that data were extracted.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 20 full-text exclusions are cited by reference number with their reasons in the running text (Results › Identification of studies, 2nd paragraph). The reason counts sum to 26 for 20 articles, so several were excluded on more than one ground; this is not explained but each exclusion has a stated reason.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives n, design, alcohol dose, BAC at testing, hangover measure, tasks and main finding; age, sex mix, setting and the interval between drinking and testing are missing.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The RevMan risk-of-bias tool was applied (results in Figure 2, an image), but blinding was deliberately not assessed, and for the naturalistic studies, which are non-randomized comparisons, no confounding domain was assessed (sleep, food, smoking, expectation). The text reports only randomization of condition order, selective reporting and other bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: The model is not named (inverse-variance weights are described, which in RevMan may be fixed or random effects) despite I2 up to 84%; how g was computed for within-person designs is not described; laboratory and naturalistic designs were pooled together with no separate estimates or stated justification.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No sensitivity analysis by risk of bias or by design.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion names non-randomized condition and task order, uncontrolled nicotine and variable sleep as limits that make firm conclusions difficult. It applies these limits mainly to explain null results (insensitive tasks, low power) rather than to the positive ones.

I2 is reported for each pool and possible sources (task sensitivity, laboratory against naturalistic design, dose, auditory against visual stimuli) are discussed, but none was investigated, although the authors themselves observe that naturalistic studies tended to find impairments and laboratory studies did not.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the authors' interests are declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (9: risk-of-bias assessment without blinding or confounding; 11: model not stated and designs pooled together; 15: publication bias not assessed), two are partly met (2 and 4) and two met (7 and 13), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. In practice the pooled numbers are averages of four or five small studies of mixed design, possibly from a fixed-effect model whose intervals would then be too narrow given the heterogeneity, with no check for missing null studies, and the strict inclusion criteria excluded several null studies. The review may be cited for the direction of next-day effects on memory, sustained attention and reaction time in controlled studies, and for the absence of pooled evidence on driving and executive function; its effect sizes should be cited as approximate and from small studies.

key_findings.finding: 805 records were screened, 39 full texts assessed, 19 studies included in the systematic review and 11 in at least one meta-analysis; 1163 participants were recruited across the 19 studies and 846 had data reported (27.3% attrition).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Results › Identification of studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Sustained attention: five studies (three laboratory, two naturalistic), three reporting impairment and two not; pooled over four studies, Hedges' g = 0.47 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.87), I2 = 50%, P = 0.02, worse after heavy drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Attention › Sustained attention, 1st paragraph; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Divided attention: five studies, of which only one (n = 5) found impairment; the meta-analysis of four studies showed no evidence of a next-day effect (no estimate reported). One study each of vigilance (no effect) and selective attention (slower responses and more Stroop interference) were not pooled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Attention › Divided attention, 1st paragraph; Results › Attention › Other attention, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Short-term memory: seven studies, three reporting impairment (one in women only) and four not; pooled over five studies, g = 0.64 (0.15 to 1.13), I2 = 73%, P = 0.01.
key_findings.locator: Results › Memory › Short-term memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend

key_findings.finding: Long-term memory: four studies; impairment in the three word-recall studies, no effect where lecture material had been learned while sober (Howland et al., 2010); pooled g = 0.59 (0.01 to 1.17), I2 = 84%, P = 0.05.
key_findings.locator: Results › Memory › Long-term memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 5 legend

key_findings.finding: Working memory was mixed: no next-day effect on the adaptive paced auditory serial addition test or auditory digit span backwards, impairment on visual span backwards in one study; not pooled.

Psychomotor speed (reaction time): three naturalistic studies found slower responses and three laboratory studies did not; pooled over five studies, g = 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00), I2 = 36%, P < 0.001. The one laboratory study that could not be pooled (Kruisselbrink et al., 2006) found no change in reaction time but lower accuracy, and the authors say its omission may inflate the estimate.
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychomotor performance › Speed, 1st paragraph; Figure 6 legend; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Real-life simulations were not pooled: no clear effect on solving a mechanical failure in a ship simulator, on managerial simulations, or on graduate record examination scores; in three naturalistic driving studies, vehicle control (deviation from a set course) was impaired in two (Laurell and Törnros, 1983; Verster et al., 2014) and speed did not change in one (Törnros and Laurell, 1991).

Naturalistic studies involved more alcohol than laboratory studies (means in the exposure field) and were more likely to find next-day impairment; the authors read this as higher amounts being linked to greater impairment, without a formal analysis.

Risk of bias (Figure 2): one study did not randomize condition order, selective reporting was unclear for every study because none was preregistered, half had other risks (non-randomized task order, sampling), and blinding was not assessed because participants readily guess their condition.
key_findings.locator: Results › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: The authors state that people in the hangover conditions may not have had hangover symptoms and that, since studies did not analyse them separately, the review examines next-day effects of heavy drinking rather than hangover as such.

Limitations named by the authors: condition order not randomized in one study and task order in three; nicotine not controlled in three; and the time between drinking and testing, and so the sleep allowed, varied between studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 1163 participants across 19 studies were included in the analysis; the Results give 846 participants with data, and only 11 studies entered any meta-analysis.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Methods; Results › Identification of studies, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed sample is smaller than the abstract implies; the pooled estimates rest on four or five studies each.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence giving 11 studies with sufficient data for meta-analysis cites only eight reference numbers (1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12), and the sustained-attention section says four studies were pooled while citing two (1, 7). The divided-attention, memory and speed sections name ten different pooled studies in all.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Identification of studies, 2nd paragraph; Results › Attention › Sustained attention
reporting_issues.consequence: The set of pooled studies cannot be fully reconstructed from the text; Figure 3, which would show it, is an image.

reporting_issues.issue: Design classification differs between places. The text counts 11 laboratory and 8 naturalistic studies, lists Verster et al. (2003) in both groups and Kim et al. (2003) as laboratory; Table 1 classes 9 studies as laboratory and 10 as naturalistic, with both of these naturalistic; the memory sections class Verster et al. (2003) as laboratory.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Results › Memory
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements contrasting laboratory and naturalistic results cannot be checked exactly; Table 1 is taken as authoritative.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives an implausible alcohol dose for Collins and Chiles, about ten times the other laboratory doses (the Discussion's range for these studies points to a misplaced decimal point; values in the exposure field), dates the study 1979 while reference 18 is 1980, and spells two author names differently from the reference list (Mrysten for Myrsten, Rohers for Roehrs).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting errors; the dose should not be quoted from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Discussion, 4th paragraph, says the laboratory reaction-time studies had 8 to 12 participants; Table 1 gives 15, 11 and 12 for the three laboratory reaction-time studies (Myrsten, Collins and Chiles, Kruisselbrink).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the point that the laboratory studies were small stands.

reporting_issues.issue: The risk-of-bias method is cited as reference 56, which is an EEG study of binge drinking (Stock et al., 2016), not a risk-of-bias tool.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Reference 56
reporting_issues.consequence: The tool is identifiable only as RevMan's risk-of-bias graph; its domains are not stated in full.

reporting_issues.issue: Two included studies did not meet the stated near-zero blood alcohol criterion for all participants (Törnros and Laurell, 1991, at their earliest morning session; four participants in Verster et al., 2014, retained after correspondence with the authors).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 and its footnotes a and b
reporting_issues.consequence: Some residual intoxication may contribute to the driving findings; the authors report that excluding the four participants did not change the Verster et al. result.

reporting_issues.issue: The meta-analysis model (fixed or random effects) is not named, and no pooled estimate is given for divided attention.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data analysis; Results › Attention › Divided attention
reporting_issues.consequence: If fixed-effect, the intervals are too narrow given I2 of 50% to 84%; the null for divided attention cannot be quantified.
